title: Conscience (CCC 1776–1782)
hookLine: the inner sanctuary where we are alone with God; Newman drank to conscience first

cards: England. A former prime minister, William Gladstone, publishes a pamphlet saying Catholics can't be loyal citizens: they've handed their consciences to the pope.
The answer comes from John Henry Newman, a well-known convert, later a cardinal and a saint. His reply is long and careful, and near the end of one section he writes a line that is still quoted.
If he ever had to bring religion into after-dinner toasts, he says, he'd drink to the pope, if you please, but "to Conscience first, and to the Pope afterwards." A cardinal, putting conscience first.

teach.b: The Second Vatican Council, which the Catechism quotes, describes conscience as a person's most secret core, a sanctuary where they are alone with God, whose voice echoes in their depths.
Not a committee, not the loudest opinion in the room: a place where you stand before God with no one else there.

teach.h: A LAW WRITTEN IN THE HEART.
teach.b: Paul says that even people who never received the law of Moses show "the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness."
The Catechism says conscience is that inner law: it calls a person to love, to do good and avoid evil, and it judges particular choices, before they're made and after. Why did Newman put it first?
In the same letter he calls conscience "the aboriginal Vicar of Christ": the first, original representative of Christ in every human being, older than any office.
And the Catechism says a person must always follow the certain judgment of their conscience. Now the part that's easy to skip. Newman wasn't praising doing whatever you feel.
Conscience has rights, he said, because it has duties.
The Catechism teaches that conscience must be formed: by Scripture, prayer, advice, the Church's teaching, and honest self-examination.
An unformed conscience can be wrong, and the Church says people are responsible for forming it. So conscience isn't a way around the truth. It's the place where you meet it, alone, and answer.

how: Catholics form their conscience through Scripture, prayer, the Church's teaching and advice, and some make a nightly examination of conscience, looking back over the day before sleep and before confession.

games.q: you're Newman. Gladstone says Catholics can't be loyal because they've handed their consciences to the pope. how do you answer?
o: agree, and say conscience doesn't matter.
say conscience comes first, and explain why it has duties.
games.why: Newman wrote a long reply and drank, in a well-known line, to conscience first, and to the pope afterwards.

practice: Bring one decision waiting for you into the quiet, big or small: a conversation, a purchase, how to spend tonight. Set aside what others will think and what's easiest, and ask only: what is the good thing to do here?
You may not hear an answer yet; the listening is the practice, and if you pray, you can ask God for light.

wordCard.voice: Conscience. The inner sanctuary where a person is alone with God, and the judgment that calls us to do good and avoid evil, formed over a lifetime.

orig.note: Greek: conscience, literally knowing-with. Latin conscientia says the same.

carryVoice: Your line: the inner sanctuary. There, the question is what's good, not what's easy. Day three hundred ten, in the books.
